awd_titl_txt: Collaborative Research: Expedite CSI Processing with Lightweight AI in Massive MIMO Communication Systems
awd_abstract_narration:
Next generation wireless communications will need to support heterogeneous devices with different capabilities on communications, computations, and power to deliver applications with various performance demands such as high data rate, low power consumption, and low latency. Massive multiple-input multiple output (MIMO) has been widely considered a compelling technology for achieving high capacity and high spectrum efficiency in the future wireless communication networks. To fully unleash the potential performance gains claimed by massive MIMO communication systems, it is of vital importance to have timely and accurate channel state information (CSI) at the transmitters, especially at the base station side. The main goal of this project is to explore a systematic approach that accelerates the CSI processing by orders of magnitude in massive MIMO communication systems. The project will lay a foundation to enhancing data rate and energy efficiency, spectral efficiency in the next-generation wireless communications. The research efforts associated with the project can have a significant impact on the lightweight artificial intelligence (AI) design for wireless communication systems, which will further improve many application domains, including beyond 5G wireless networks, autonomous machine-to-machine communications, vehicular networks, and Internet-of-Things. The outcomes of the project can foster the transition of our society into the intelligent wireless networking age, where wireless communication systems can provide seamless support to match many different wireless applications for massive network devices and support many services with high computation demands and quality of service needs. Moreover, the Principal Investigators are committed to integrating research and education by introducing emerging computing and lightweight AI in wireless communication systems into the current electrical and computer engineering curricula in the three participating universities. The project will also provide opportunities for students to learn, develop and apply advanced wireless communications, which they would not receive from a traditional B.S. or M.S. curriculum.

Meeting the coherence time requirement in massive MIMO systems can be extremely difficult for CSI processing due to the complex traditional model as well as AI model development and inconsistent performance across environments. In this research project, theoretical analysis and performance evaluations will be obtained for novel algorithms designed for 1) optimization on the decompressed feature in the CSI reconstruction process, 2) simplifying the AI structures for multi-rate compression and reconstruction, and 3) autonomous CSI reconstruction performance evaluation and AI model update. The optimized features and simplified AI structures can significantly reduce the complexity in terms of floating point operations per second (FLOPs). Thus, the AI implementation can be accelerated by 1 to 2 orders of magnitude without losing reconstruction accuracy for timely CSI processing in massive MIMO communication systems. The systematic methodologies can be readily extended to facilitate many other applications that encounter the similar challenges and present similar needs on reducing latency and computation needs. Furthermore, this research project can greatly promote the understanding in AI-supported massive MIMO systems for better spectrum and power efficiency and will contribute fundamentally to the design of highly efficient machine-to-machine communications that require high level of autonomy.

This award reflects NSF's statutory mission and has been deemed worthy of support through evaluation using the Foundation's intellectual merit and broader impacts review criteria.

por.por_cntn:
This project advanced an AI‑supported wireless communication paradigm to meet rapidly growing throughput demands while sustaining ultra‑low latency. The central objective was to accelerate AI‑enabled channel state information (CSI) processing in massive multiple‑input multiple‑output (MIMO) systems by 1-2 orders of magnitude without compromising reconstruction fidelity. The project delivered an integrated suite of algorithms, evaluation platforms, and design principles that reduce CSI acquisition and feedback overhead, improve robustness under environmental dynamics, and improve spectrum efficiency for next‑generation wireless networks. Overall, the research demonstrates strong potential to enhance massive MIMO system design and to establish a new AI‑assisted framework that can substantially improve CSI processing in future wireless systems.

Over four years, the project addressed key challenges in massive MIMO, focusing on CSI processing and spectrum management. The work developed and evaluated AI‑supported channel estimation and CSI feedback mechanisms, and connected these innovations to spectrum efficiency and quality‑of‑service (QoS)‑aware resource management. Major research outcomes include the following:

(1) Extensible evaluation platform for MIMO channel estimation and CSI feedback: An extensible software platform was created to evaluate MIMO channel estimation and CSI feedback under consistent conditions. The platform supports side‑by‑side comparisons among least‑squares estimation, compressive‑sensing‑based feedback, and deep learning autoencoder approaches. Using mean squared error (MSE) and bit error rate (BER) as primary metrics, the platform enables systematic assessment of accuracy, latency and overhead tradeoffs across antenna array sizes, pilot configurations, and precoding choices. This platform served as the experimental backbone for subsequent algorithm and architecture development.

(2) Redesigned AI architecture for CSI feedback in FDD massive MIMO: A redesigned AI architecture was developed for CSI feedback in frequency division duplex (FDD) massive MIMO. Specifically, an autoencoder was designed to process received pilot sequences directly, thereby reducing error accumulation typically introduced by separate estimation and compression stages. The resulting design supports higher compression ratios while maintaining strong CSI reconstruction quality and improving BER performance. This architecture also increases robustness to practical estimation imperfections.

(3) Latency‑aware CSI processing under high mobility:  Processing latency can become a dominant impairment in high‑mobility settings. This effect was studied in orthogonal time frequency space (OTFS) massive MIMO systems, where delay, Doppler, and angle parameters may evolve during estimation and feedback. A latency‑explicit analysis of uplink‑aided downlink channel estimation quantified how even modest delays can induce index shifts, leading to substantial downlink estimation error. The results clarify operating regimes in which uplink assistance remains reliable and motivate latency‑reduction and tracking strategies for vehicular and other high‑speed scenarios.

(4) Reliability under data distribution shift via open‑set recognition and adaptation: AI‑based CSI models often assume a fixed training distribution, and performance can degrade when deployment environments differ from training conditions. To address this, a two‑stage open‑set recognition framework was introduced. The first stage detects previously unseen environments using reconstruction‑error signatures, while the second stage filters and organizes newly collected data to enable lightweight, autonomous adaptation. This approach improves reliability under distribution shift without requiring costly retraining pipelines.

(5) Beamforming performance in complex indoor multipath environments: Beamforming was evaluated in challenging indoor multipath scenarios. Results indicate that directional‑path‑only beamforming can be suboptimal when line‑of‑sight is blocked, highlighting the need for environment‑aware strategies that exploit richer multipath structure rather than relying solely on dominant directional components.

(6) System‑level integration: At the system level, CSI processing innovations were linked to spectrum efficiency and QoS‑aware resource management. One contribution integrated spectrum sensing into the channel estimation workflow, enabling adjacent‑band occupancy detection through the same processing pipeline used for channel estimation. This integration reduces latency and avoids reliance on separate sensing hardware. In parallel, model‑based deep learning methods were developed for QoS‑aware rate‑splitting multiple access (RSMA) resource allocation, combining classical optimization structure with deep unfolding to accelerate convergence while preserving feasibility and improving data efficiency. Together, these efforts strengthen the pathway from CSI acquisition to real‑time spectrum management decisions.

(7) Spatial channel representations and reconfigurable intelligent surface (RIS)‑enabled 6G operation: The project also explored richer spatial channel representations and RIS‑enabled operation for 6G. A Spatial‑CSI concept was introduced to capture directional and spatial propagation characteristics, supporting improved beamforming and RIS optimization as well as digital radio‑twin‑style evaluation. The Spatial‑CSI representation was further investigated in security‑relevant settings through a study of selective multiuser jamming enabled by RIS, using a deep reinforcement learning framework.

Collectively, these outcomes advance lightweight, low‑latency AI designs for CSI processing and support more self‑sustaining, robust operation in real‑world wireless environments. The project produced reusable evaluation workflows, clarified performance limits imposed by mobility and processing latency, and delivered learning mechanisms that enhance reliability under distribution shift. These contributions are foundational for next‑generation wireless networks and particularly relevant to machine‑type communications, vehicular connectivity, and Internet‑of‑Things applications. Moreover, three PhD students and one undergraduate students have been partially trained throughout the project.
